title: One fault a year (I.11)
hookLine: a resolution list, every item starting Monday, lost by spring: chapter eleven's arithmetic is one fault a year
tomorrow: why is it easier to stop a knock than a guest already inside?
last: FEEL, NOT DEFINE · UNKNOWN · TRUTH ITSELF TEACHES.

cards: January. A fresh note on the phone: run more, read more, sleep more, scroll less, call grandma, learn guitar. Every item starting Monday.
By spring the note is buried under grocery lists. Chapter eleven of The Imitation of Christ has a different plan, and it's almost suspiciously small.
If every year we rooted out one vice, it says, we would soon be perfect. One. Not the whole list.
Then the chapter admits why even one is hard.

teach.h: BETTER AT THE START THAN YEARS LATER.
teach.b: Here's the honest part. Often, the chapter says, it goes the other way: people were better and purer at the start of their conversion than after many years.
Fervor should grow every day; instead, it seems a great thing to keep even part of the first fire. And its fix is about timing.
If we pushed against ourselves a little at the beginning, it says, we could afterward do everything with ease and joy. It's hard to give up what you're used to.
But if you don't overcome small, easy things, how will you overcome the hard ones? So pick one, and lean hardest at the start. That's this week, too.
Feel the sting instead of defining it. Do the good no one sees. Let truth teach you firsthand.
Weigh the rumor. Seek the plain truth. Take the counsel.

teach.h: SIX LINES, ONE AT A TIME.
teach.b: Six lines, and chapter eleven's quiet suggestion: don't try all six by Monday.

how: Some Catholics practice a particular examen, a daily look at one chosen fault, and bring their struggles to confession.

games.q: what does “one fault a year” mean?
o: rooting out one fault at a time, pushing at the start
a single sin each year that can never be forgiven
the one mistake a team is allowed in a whole season

games.q: this week's lines — tap the pairs.

s: the Imitation says you can fix every fault this year if you try hard enough
it suggests one vice a year, pushing hardest at the start.
the chapter says people are sometimes better at the start of conversion than years later
and it says keeping even part of the first fervor seems a great thing.
the chapter says small faults don't matter
if you don't overcome small, easy things, how will you overcome harder ones?

games.q: your dad writes ten habits to fix this month and is already discouraged on day three. what does chapter eleven suggest?
o: pick one, and push hardest at the beginning.
keep all ten; more effort means faster change.
drop the list; small faults don't really matter.
games.why: one vice rooted out a year, the chapter says, and a little force against yourself at the start makes the rest come with ease.

practice: Name one fault, just one, you'd like gone by this time next year. Picture the moment it usually shows up, and decide the one small thing you'll do in that moment instead. Then rest, with the plan made.

wordCard.voice: One fault a year. Chapter eleven's slow arithmetic: root out one vice at a time, pushing hardest at the start.
